## Home — https://www.yasassri.me/

Dr. Yasas Sri Wickramasinghe — Postdoctoral Researcher · Senior Lecturer.

**About.** Collaborating at the intersection of spatial interfaces and human
behavior. I'm Dr. Yasas Sri Wickramasinghe — a Postdoctoral Researcher at HIT
Lab NZ (University of Canterbury) and Senior Lecturer at Yoobee College of
Creative Innovation. I hold a PhD in Human Interface Technology, with a
dissertation on designing multiplayer location-based AR games that connect
remote players and places. My work is conducted with industry partners
including Sony Interactive Entertainment (Japan) and Niantic, Inc. Earlier I
co-founded NavitaZ VR Labs under the MIT Global Startup Labs programme and led
Sri Lanka's first large-scale MOOC platform. Research partners: HIT Lab NZ,
Sony Interactive Entertainment, and Niantic Spatial.

**Academic Platform — work with me directly.** Consultations, speaking
invitations, writing, and a student community, in one place, at
yasassri.me/app: Book a Free Consultation (30–45 min on education, research or
career guidance, no charge) — Invite Me to Speak (signature talks, a
ready-to-use speaker kit, and invitations, at yasassri.me/speaking.html) —
Read the Blog (writing on HCI, AR/VR,
software engineering and education) — Join the Forum (ask questions, help
peers, stay connected as a community).

**Three research frontiers.** (1) Location-Based AR — designing multiplayer AR
experiences that meaningfully connect remote players to real-world places. (2)
Spatial Computing & XR — studying how immersive interfaces reshape cognition,
trust, and decision-making in shared spaces. (3) Player Experience & HCI —
evaluating how people feel, behave, and collaborate inside the systems we
design and deploy. Research notes, occasionally: notes on immersive media,
spatial computing, and lessons from building XR — a few times a year.

**Selected work.** Representing Remote Locations with Location-Based AR Game
Design — Entertainment Computing, Elsevier, 2025. A multiplayer
location-based AR system, designed and evaluated with Sony Interactive
Entertainment, exploring how players experience and represent distant
real-world places together — published across leading HCI venues.

**New book — The Collaboration Reflex.** "Why the 'right' answer to conflict
is usually wrong." Conflict shows up in every team, every project, every
workplace — and almost everyone reaches for the same answer: collaborate,
find the win-win. This book argues that reflex is usually wrong, using
forty-five real, anonymised workplace conflicts to show when collaboration
works, when it backfires, and what to do instead. Free download at
yasassri.me/app/#/book; sign-in required, takes under a minute.

**Upcoming talks & workshops.** Three engagements on the calendar, or invite
me for something similar: Designing Shared Worlds Across Distance (NZGDC,
1 October 2026) — Presenting on VR Presence & Motion Sickness (VRST 2026,
Sendai, Japan, 16–18 November 2026) — ICITR 2026 Workshop 01: Designing Shared Worlds Across
Distance (University of Moratuwa, date to be announced). Full details at
yasassri.me/news.html.

**Just wrapped.** Talks and workshops delivered this year, with the material
and demos still online: From Research to Reality — AR/VR Entrepreneurship
Opportunities (IEEE Entrepreneurship, Sri Lanka, 22 September 2026) — Code Champ 2026 Workshop 07: Augmented Reality and Game
Development (20 August 2026) — CODE with WIE 2026 Workshop 01: Architecting
the Augmented Tomorrow (IEEE WIE Sri Lanka, 11 July 2026).

**In the news.** Invited talks, international collaborations and outreach —
where the research meets people and places: Research Visit to Tohoku
University — an NZ–Japan AR collaboration (Tohoku University, Dec 2025) —
Breaking the Wall of Loneliness Through Play (Royal Society Te Apārangi,
2024) — Talking AR Game Design on the National Stage (NZGDC 2023 panel).

**What I do.** Research & Publications — peer-reviewed work in AR, XR and HCI,
from study design and experimental platforms to journal and conference
papers. Teaching & Supervision — Master's-level courses in information
systems and project management, plus capstone and thesis supervision,
gamified and high-engagement. XR & Software Development — building immersive
prototypes and production systems with Unity, OpenXR and Niantic Lightship.
Talks & Consulting — consulting, team workshops and keynotes on immersive
technology, XR user research and engaged learning, evidence-led with a fixed
scope agreed up front (yasassri.me/work-with-me.html).

**FAQ.**
Q: Who is Dr. Yasas Sri Wickramasinghe? A: Dr. Yasas Sri Wickramasinghe is an
augmented reality researcher, university lecturer and software engineer based
in Christchurch, New Zealand. He is a Postdoctoral Researcher at HIT Lab NZ
(University of Canterbury) and a Senior Lecturer at Yoobee College of
Creative Innovation.
Q: What does Yasas Sri Wickramasinghe research? A: His research focuses on
location-based augmented reality (AR), spatial computing and
human-computer interaction (HCI) — in particular multiplayer AR games that
connect remote players and places, conducted with industry partners
including Sony Interactive Entertainment and Niantic.
Q: Where does he teach? A: He is a Senior Lecturer at Yoobee College of
Creative Innovation, teaching postgraduate information systems and project
management, including the Master of Business Informatics (MBI) programme
across the Auckland and Christchurch campuses.
Q: What web products has he built? A: He has designed and built HouseScout (a
property-intelligence dashboard for Christchurch home buyers), PathFinder (a
planning platform for Sri Lankan students applying to postgraduate study in
New Zealand) and Faro (a machine-learning flight-fare timing assistant). See
yasassri.me/products.html.
Q: How can I get in touch? A: Via the contact page at yasassri.me/contact.html
for research collaborations, guest talks, consulting and academic mentorship.

### Founder — ICT Campus and Campus Ready

Dr. Yasas Sri Wickramasinghe founded ICT Campus (https://ictcampus.lk) and is
its lead teacher: an online tuition platform for Sri Lankan A/L ICT students in
Grades 12 and 13, in Sinhala and English medium, covering the full NIE
syllabus, with live classes, recordings, timed mock exams, a Code Lab, free
notes and past papers, and a free 7-day trial.

Campus Ready (https://ictcampus.lk/campus-ready) is ICT Campus's second
initiative: a 12-week programme, taught in Sinhala, for students waiting
between their A/Ls and university. It covers Word, Excel, Python, statistics,
Power BI, referencing, Zotero and ethical AI use, ending in a capstone
dashboard on real Sri Lankan open data and a graded, verifiable certificate
(issued by ICT Campus; not university-accredited). Intakes in January and
July; first intake January 2027.

## Research — https://www.yasassri.me/research.html

Connecting players & places across distance. My research designs, builds, and
evaluates location-based augmented reality games that let physically
separated players share a single augmented space. Through a
research-through-design approach, I study how AR can move beyond decoration to
become a core mechanic — reframing place itself as a shared, interactive
canvas across distance.

**The driving question.** "How can augmented reality make meaningful use of
the real world to facilitate synchronous remote multiplayer gameplay?" Most
location-based AR games treat AR as an optional visual layer — players can
often switch it off without changing the game. My doctoral research asks the
opposite: what happens when AR becomes the mechanism that binds remote places
and players together? I answer this across three empirical user studies,
organised around three research questions on representing remote space,
spatial decision-making, and interactive AR mechanics. Snapshot: 3 empirical
user studies, 128 study participants, 5 peer-reviewed articles, 4
design-guideline themes.

**Doctoral thesis.** "Designing Multiplayer Location-Based Augmented Reality
Games that Connect Remote Players and Places" — PhD, University of
Canterbury, HIT Lab NZ. Supervised by Prof. Stephan Lukosch, A. Prof. Heide
Lukosch, and James Everett, this thesis uses an iterative
research-through-design method — cycles of design, development, and
evaluation — to investigate how AR can represent remote spaces, support
spatial decision-making, and drive engagement through core game mechanics.
The work spans five peer-reviewed publications (Articles I–V) and contributes
theoretically, empirically, methodologically, and practically to the design
of remote multiplayer AR games. UC Research Repository:
https://ir.canterbury.ac.nz/items/6df971c0-1314-4863-8156-304c838686d0

**Three studies.** Study 01 (RQ1) — Representing Remote Spaces: compared three
AR techniques — Overlay, Window, and Tabletop — for portraying a remote
location. Overlay produced the strongest sense of "being there" and
self-location; Window felt like the remote place extending into your own;
Tabletop offered a detached strategic overview. 30 participants; Entertainment
Computing. Study 02 (RQ2) — Decision-Making & Experience: a remote multiplayer
AR hide-and-seek game compared against co-located play. AR shifted spatial
strategies — players exploited mid-air and vertical space — and a lightweight
frustum cue strengthened social connection without avatars or video. 60
participants; IEEE VR, MDPI MTI. Study 03 (RQ3) — Mechanics & Constraints:
introduced interactive core AR mechanics — real-time object manipulation,
particle-effect feedback, and time pressure. These deepened strategic search
behaviour and engagement when paired with clear feedback and well-calibrated
constraints. 38 participants; OzCHI 2025.

**Design guidelines.** (1) Remote Space Representation — make the place feel
present: prioritise real-world-scale Overlay views for spatial presence, use
Window "portals" as an intuitive interface for sharing resources between
locations, ground it all in high-fidelity 3D scans of the remote environment.
(2) Player Interaction & Coordination — lightweight presence beats fidelity:
visualise the remote player's viewpoint in real time and add voice; minimal
orientation cues (a frustum avatar) coordinated players as effectively as far
heavier embodiment. (3) AR Mechanics & Constraints — AR as a core mechanic:
embed AR in the gameplay loop rather than as decoration — multiple remotely
anchored objects, real-time manipulation, carefully calibrated time pressure.
(4) Engagement & Spatial Decisions — guide without removing the challenge:
subtle feedback (like particle trails marking object swaps) supports
orientation while preserving discovery; support onboarding to reduce early
disorientation; design for player safety during physical movement.

**Other projects.** Trust in Shared Augmented Reality (ACM SUI 2024) —
investigating how design choices shape trust when users exchange virtual
items in shared AR environments; a 36-participant study presented at the ACM
Symposium on Spatial User Interaction 2024. NavitaZ VR Labs (2015–2019) —
co-founded an AR/VR startup under the MIT Global Startup Labs programme; built
mobile AR apps and VR web applications in Sri Lanka; Microsoft Imagine Cup
Runner-Up 2015.

## Teaching — https://www.yasassri.me/teaching.html

Building the future of learning. I design experiential, technology-forward
classrooms — and build the platforms that power them. My Master's programme teaching is inseparable from the state-of-the-art learning management system I built to bring attendance, live coding, competitive SQL, and AI-assisted
reasoning into every session.

**A state-of-the-art learning management system — the platform I built.** A real-time learning platform: a full-stack web application I designed and built from scratch for the Master of Business Informatics (MBI) courses I teach. It
replaces static slide decks and paper registers with a live, interactive,
data-driven classroom experience. Every feature was shaped by a real
classroom problem — from fraudulent attendance submissions caught by three
detection algorithms, to students competing on SQL queries in real time.
Stack: React 18, TypeScript 5, Vite 5, Tailwind CSS 3, Firebase Auth,
Firestore, Firebase Storage. Open-source on GitHub (github.com/ureshan2011).
Snapshot stats: 228 students across 3 courses, 24 countries in cohorts,
2,500+ attendance records logged, 100+ quiz MCQs and 16 lecture videos.

Features: One-tap Attendance with fraud detection — students check in with a
single tap; three detection algorithms run in real time to flag dishonest
submissions: shared-IP clustering (multiple students on one device), GPS
outlier detection (coordinates >500 m from campus), and a rapid-submission
window (check-ins within 30 s of session open). Live Playground — an
in-browser code execution environment embedded directly in lectures; students
write and run SQL, Python snippets, and pseudocode without leaving the
platform. SQL Race — students race around a virtual track by solving SQL
challenges in sequence: SELECT → WHERE → JOIN → GROUP BY → ORDER BY → HAVING;
a live leaderboard drives friendly competition. Quiz Badges — over 100 MCQ
questions across all three MBI courses; students earn badge tiers as they
progress, with instant feedback and explanations. Daily Match — a daily
collaborative challenge pairs students across cohorts to solve a shared
problem together, building cross-cultural communication skills across 24
countries. Cohort Analytics — a lecturer-only dashboard surfaces attendance
trends, quiz completion rates, country-level engagement, and fraud alert
history.

**SQL Race — feature spotlight.** SQL Race transforms database exercises
into a live, multiplayer competition. Each checkpoint on the track
corresponds to a core SQL clause. Students only advance by writing a correct
query. It was born out of a simple observation: students who were bored by
textbook drills became intensely focused the moment there was a leaderboard.
Checkpoints: 01 Select (basic column retrieval), 02 Where (row-level
filtering), 03 Join (multi-table relationships), 04 Group By (aggregation
logic), 05 Order By (result sorting), 06 Having (post-aggregation filter).

**MBI course catalog** (Master of Business Informatics, New Zealand).
MBI800 — Business Information Systems (Strategy & Systems Planning): the
strategic role of information systems in organisations — IS alignment and
SISP (Strategic Information Systems Planning), digital transformation
frameworks, Porter's competitive models. Platform feature: SISP Prompt Lab —
an AI-assisted tool embedded in the LMS that walks students through strategic
IS planning exercises using guided prompts and real case data.
MBI802 — Database Management Systems (SQL, ER Modelling, NoSQL): a hands-on
deep-dive into relational database design, SQL from basics to advanced joins
and stored procedures, ER diagram methodology, normalisation theory, and an
introduction to NoSQL paradigms. Platform features: SQL Race (competitive
live query challenges) and Live Playground (in-browser SQL execution
environment).
MBI804 — IT Project Management (Agile, Scrum, Risk): the full project
lifecycle — initiation, planning, execution, monitoring, and closure — with a
strong practical emphasis on Agile methodologies, Scrum ceremonies,
stakeholder management, and risk frameworks. Platform feature: Case Study
Labs — students manage a simulated IT project via the LMS, tracking sprints,
updating risk registers, and submitting deliverables with structured peer
review.

**Teaching philosophy.** My approach to education is grounded in experiential
and constructivist learning — I believe students learn best by building,
failing, iterating, and reflecting. Every feature in the LMS was designed
around this principle: the Live Playground lowers the barrier to trying, SQL
Race makes failure feel like just one more lap, and badge tiers reward
persistence over perfection. I prioritise purpose-driven education: helping
students not just acquire technical skills, but develop the vision and
initiative to use them meaningfully. In a classroom spanning 24 countries,
that also means building cultural fluency and collaborative communication
into every assignment. "If we can change the way we see the world, we can
change the world we see." Availability: Mon–Sat, 10:00–17:00, in-person /
virtual, at Christchurch, NZ, for mentoring, supervision, and
industry talks.

**Previous teaching.** 2021–2022 — Computer Architecture & Enterprise
Software, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka. 2018–2021 — Database Management
Systems, SLIIT & University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka. 2018–2022 —
Human-Computer Interaction, University of Moratuwa & SLIIT, Sri Lanka.
2018–2022 — Project Management & Enterprise App Development, SLIIT, Sri
Lanka.

"The classroom is not a place where knowledge is delivered — it's a space
where thinking is provoked." — Dr. Yasas Sri Wickramasinghe, Lecturer, Master of Business Informatics.

**FAQ.** Q: What master's programme does he teach? A: The
Master of Business Informatics (MBI) — MBI800 Business Information Systems,
MBI802 Database Management Systems, and MBI804 IT Project Management, across
the Auckland and Christchurch campuses. Q: Is this an official college page? A: No — this page is his own account of the courses he teaches, not an
official college page; for admissions, fees or enrolment, contact the college directly. Q: I'm considering applying — where
can I learn more? A: See his guide for prospective students
(yasassri.me/students.html) for programme facts, his teaching approach, and a
free consultation link.

### Teaching in Sri Lanka

Before New Zealand I was a Lecturer at the University of Moratuwa's Faculty
of Information Technology (2018–2022), teaching object-oriented programming,
multimedia and web technologies, computer architecture and enterprise
software, databases and HCI, and supervising research. I was also a visiting
lecturer at NSBM Green University, SLIIT and the Institute of Technology,
University of Moratuwa (ITUM), and Platform Lead for the Software Engineering
strand of the University of Moratuwa's open learning platform (open.uom.lk),
which reached 150,000+ registered learners. Today I teach A/L ICT to Grade 12
and 13 students in Sri Lanka through ICT Campus (https://ictcampus.lk), the online
classroom I founded. Classes are live, in Sinhala and English medium, and
follow the NIE syllabus. Free study material, no account needed: the A/L ICT
syllabus (https://ictcampus.lk/syllabus), past papers
(https://ictcampus.lk/past-papers), short notes, exam command words, logic
gates, number systems and a revision plan. For the wait between A/Ls and
university: Campus Ready (https://ictcampus.lk/campus-ready), a 12-week
course, plus free guides on what to do after A/Ls
(https://ictcampus.lk/after-al), the Z-score (https://ictcampus.lk/z-score),
university Z-score cut-offs (https://ictcampus.lk/z-score-cutoffs), the UGC
application, APA referencing and using AI in assignments. Teacher profile:
https://ictcampus.lk/dr-yasas

## Lessons — https://www.yasassri.me/lessons.html

Blended Teaching Content is the set of 40 interactive lessons Dr. Yasas Sri Wickramasinghe built for the four Master of Business Informatics (MBI) courses he teaches: MBI800, MBI802, MBI804 and MBI806B. The lessons are hosted on his lessons site (https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/) and open free in any browser, with no login and nothing to install; the lessons page on this site showcases and links to every one. Lessons are simulations, labs, practice sets and knowledge checks in which every wrong answer is explained. Synced from the lessons site's course registry on 2026-09-28.

### MBI800 — Strategic Information Systems Planning (9 lessons)

Course home: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/mbi800
The course runs from a single system to a whole industry: systems thinking first, then five platforms that rewired their markets, then what it costs when security is an afterthought.

- Introduction and systems thinking (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/intro-to-sisp.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/intro-to-sisp) — The whole of Lesson 1: what strategic planning actually decides, systems against collections, a sales loop you can run for twelve months to watch the obvious fix rebound, and the Iceberg Model taken down through a real outage. Ends with a knowledge check.
- The Business Model Canvas (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/business-model-canvas.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/business-model-canvas) — How a business model works, laid out on one page in nine blocks. Then a 90-minute group activity: six people, one IT business idea, a canvas filled in digitally and presented as a short slide deck.
- Threats to opportunities to strategy (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/threats-to-strategy.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/threats-to-strategy) — How a business capitalises on its threats. Netflix, Apple, Adobe, Microsoft, NZ Post and Google each turned a threat into a strategy, Kodak and Fujifilm took the same threat two ways, then you flip six threats yourself.
- Five stories that changed everything (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/five-stories.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/five-stories) — Airbnb, Netflix, Xero, Canva and Alibaba — how each started from one frustration and built a platform that rewired its industry. IS architecture, growth figures and discussion questions for each.
- Platform strategy (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/platform-strategy.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/platform-strategy) — Why Uber owns no cars and the App Store writes no apps. Network effects, the chicken-and-egg problem, governance and boundary resources, Amazon against GE Predix — then a group research task and a knowledge check.
- Systems security (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/systems-security.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/systems-security) — What can go wrong, what it would cost, and how to defend and recover. Calculate real risk exposure, profile the attackers, tell malware apart, run a backup simulator and choose a disaster-recovery plan.
- Immersive realities (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/xr-explorer.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/xr-explorer) — A walk through AR, VR and mixed reality, with two demos that run in the browser. No headset needed, and no prior graphics knowledge assumed.
- Capstone: shipping your own site (Lab): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/bonus-lecture.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/bonus-lecture) — The final lecture. Design a layout in Google Stitch, turn it into real code with Claude Code, and put it live on GitHub Pages. Includes a prompt generator for your own portfolio.
- The written study pack (Pack): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/study-packs.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/study-packs) — The whole course rewritten as a properly typeset book: eleven chapters, worked examples, practice questions and answer keys. Yours to download and keep.

### MBI802 — Database Management Systems (17 lessons)

Course home: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/mbi802
Each lesson assumes the one before it. SQL before diagrams, diagrams before mapping, mapping before normalisation — that order is the course, not a filing system.

- Introduction to DBMS (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/intro-to-dbms.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/intro-to-dbms) — Break a hospital's spreadsheet and watch it contradict itself, turn a bare number into information, then read the full eight-lesson outline with a preview of the material. Nothing to install.
- Setting up MySQL (Video): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/mysql-setup.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/mysql-setup) — Two short guide videos — one for MacOS, one for Windows — so your MySQL client and Workbench are installed and ready before the first hands-on class.
- Introduction to SQL with MySQL (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/app/lessons/sql-programming.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/sql-programming) — The language databases actually speak. Create a database, build a table, insert real rows, then ask it questions — one interactive slide at a time.
- Advanced database concepts (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/app/lessons/database-concepts.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/database-concepts) — One table, built up step by step: add a column, change a data type, set a primary key and auto-number it, back it up and restore it, then ORDER BY and count it. Finishes with a safe look at SQL injection.
- Client, server and databases (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/web-architecture.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/web-architecture) — How a website actually works, for absolute beginners. Sort jobs between the two computers, then follow one search all the way to the database and back — watching the server run the SQL as it goes. Ends in a safe attack lab.
- ER diagrams (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/app/lessons/er-diagrams.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/er-diagrams) — Sketch the world before you build the tables. Entities, attributes and relationships in Chen's notation, and how to read cardinality at a glance.
- ER diagrams in practice (Practice): https://www.yasassri.me/app/lessons/er-activities.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/er-activities) — Model five real systems — a library, a university, a hospital, an online store and a hotel — then check your diagram against a worked answer.
- Advanced ER concepts (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/app/lessons/er-advanced.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/er-advanced) — Real data is messier than the textbook. Weak entities, identifying relationships, and multivalued or derived attributes, with two exercises to test yourself.
- Attributes and participation (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/app/lessons/er-attributes.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/er-attributes) — The details that decide whether a model is right or wrong. Break attributes into their parts, then read total against partial participation through guided activities.
- ER to relational mapping (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/er-mapping.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/er-mapping) — Turn entity-relationship diagrams into real relational tables — entities, relationships, keys, and every tricky case in between.
- Database normalisation (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/normalisation.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/normalisation) — From messy tables to clean ones. Spot the anomalies, then split a table step by step from 1NF all the way to 3NF.
- Normalisation activities (Practice): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/normalisation-activities.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/normalisation-activities) — Seven short tables to practise on, mixed up and with no hints. Work out what normal form each is in and normalise it. The answers sit behind a password so you try it first.
- Normalisation on video (Video): https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/normalisation-videos — Prefer to watch? A short walkthrough series — why we normalise, functional dependencies, and First Normal Form — each as a clip you can play any time.
- UPDATE and DELETE (Video): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/sql-reels.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/sql-reels) — Change and remove rows with confidence. Short scrollable reels that show how to edit data without breaking everything around it.
- SwiftShop security lab (Lab): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/security-lab.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/security-lab.html) — A deliberately insecure shop with twenty hidden vulnerabilities, from editable price tags and secrets in the page source to XSS, privilege escalation and business-logic flaws. Find them, exploit them, then explain the fix.
- Free SQL certifications (Reference): https://www.yasassri.me/app/lessons/sql-certifications.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/sql-certifications) — Nine genuinely free credentials — Oracle badges, IBM digital badges, HackerRank exams, Cisco certs and more. No credit card for any of them.
- The written study pack (Pack): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/study-packs.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/study-packs) — The whole course rewritten as a properly typeset book: eight chapters, worked examples, practice questions and answer keys. Yours to download and keep.

### MBI804 — IT Project Management (9 lessons)

Course home: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/mbi804
The course keeps returning to one question: which of the three constraints are you willing to move? Every estimate, every risk and every conflict on this page is another way of asking it.

- What a project is, and what decides how to run it (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/intro-to-project-management.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/intro-to-project-management) — The whole of Lesson 1: pin two corners of the constraint triangle and watch the third move, slide a delay along a real schedule to find which tasks the launch date cares about, choose between Agile, Waterfall and PRINCE2 across four project shapes, then price a risk on the grid.
- The Business Model Canvas (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/business-model-canvas.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/business-model-canvas-mbi804) — How a business model works, laid out on one page in nine blocks. Then a 90-minute group activity: six people, one IT business idea, a canvas filled in digitally and presented as a short slide deck. Shared with MBI800.
- Waterfall, Spiral, PRINCE2 and Agile — and Scrum up close (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/project-methodologies.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/project-methodologies) — Lesson 2, and the one the 60% case study leans on. Four lifecycles drawn rather than described, a change dragged along the cost-of-change curve, Boehm’s spiral walked loop by loop, PRINCE2’s seven principles, themes and processes opened one at a time, then the whole Agile family — and Scrum in full: a clickable framework diagram, twelve “whose job is this?” situations, timeboxes that scale with the Sprint, and a board with a live burndown.
- The Scrum studio: a Sprint you can watch, pause and orbit (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/scrum-simulation.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/scrum-simulation) — Lesson 3. Six 3D miniatures build a parcel drone through three one-week Sprints while a caption says what is happening and a timeline marks every milestone: the Product Backlog ordered on the wall, refined and estimated with Planning Poker, Sprint Planning pulling cards into the Sprint Backlog, a fifteen-minute Daily Scrum every morning, an impediment landing and being cleared, stakeholders watching the drone lift off at the Review, one improvement from each Retrospective. Voice-narrated, it pauses after each step so you can read, then a seven-question check.
- The outside auditor: peer audit round (Practice): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/peer-audit.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/peer-audit) — The class swaps post-mortems — you audit a project you did not run, and nobody gets their own back. Practise the four audit questions on a fictional scenario whose author is confident and wrong about all of them, sort eight sentences into restating, asserting and auditing, choose a risk response where mitigating is the wrong answer, then build the one-page Corrective Action Plan and export it.
- Project cost management (Lesson) (currently offline on the lessons site): https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/cost-management — Plan, estimate, budget — and avoid the traps that sink most IT projects. Seven interactive sections around the SecurePay NZ scenario: PERT calculator, budget builder, live S-curve and a closing challenge.
- The collaboration reflex (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/collaboration-reflex-lecture.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/collaboration-reflex-lecture.html) — Conflict and communication management taught through forty-five real, anonymised classroom conflicts: six full stories, four frameworks, and the one reflex experienced professionals reach for even when it is the wrong answer.
- Conflict swap (Practice): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/conflict-swap.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/conflict-swap.html) — Write a real conflict you have lived through, anonymously. The class shuffles everyone's stories so you analyse someone else's — root cause, the mode that was used, and the mode that should have been. A class code from me, no login.
- Free Jira and Agile certifications (Reference): https://www.yasassri.me/app/lessons/jira-certifications.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/jira-certifications) — Three hand-picked credentials: Atlassian's own Jira learning path, a LinkedIn Agile Professional Certificate, and a quick free completion cert.

### MBI806B — Business Data Analytics with AI and ML (4 lessons)

Course home: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/mbi806b
Getting a number out is the easy half. Being able to defend the number, and say what it cannot tell you, is the job this course is actually about.

- Welcome to business data analytics (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/intro-to-business-analytics.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/intro-to-business-analytics) — For absolute beginners: what AI and ML actually mean, where you already use them without noticing, how real decisions get made step by step, and a first look at Power BI.
- Setting up Python (Lab): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/python-setup.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/python-setup) — No installing, no downloads. Open Google Colab in your browser — identical on Mac and Windows — and write your first line of Python in two minutes.
- Three ways to predict things (Lesson): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/predicting-with-data.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/predicting-with-data) — Linear regression, decision trees and random forests, explained with no maths. Move a line until it fits, grow a tree until it cheats, watch nine trees outvote the best one — then run real Python in the page.
- Setting up Power BI (Lab): https://www.yasassri.me/lessons/power-bi-setup.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/power-bi-setup) — From nothing to your first chart. Everybody starts in the browser, which works the same on a Mac as on a PC — nobody should spend the first class watching a download bar.

### Shared across every course

- APA 7 citations: the crash course (Reference): https://www.yasassri.me/app/lessons/apa-referencing.html (interactive: https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/apa-referencing) — Everything needed to cite correctly, from the first in-text citation to the last reference entry. Fourteen interactive slides and a practice quiz.
- The pre-class idea swarm (Reference) (opens with a class password): https://ureshan2011.github.io/thisisnotalms/#/pre-class — A full-screen countdown for the minutes before class. Key concepts drift like a galaxy, then swarm together to reveal the course code right as we begin.

## Studying a master's in New Zealand — https://www.yasassri.me/students.html

"Studying a master's in New Zealand: what I tell my students." A long-form
guide by Dr. Yasas Sri Wickramasinghe, written as experience sharing from a
lecturer who teaches master's students in New Zealand (information systems
strategy, database management, IT project management and business analytics
in a Master of Business Informatics programme, Christchurch and Auckland) and
who came to New Zealand from Sri Lanka as a postgraduate student himself. It is
not official advice and gives no visa or immigration advice; it points readers
to Immigration New Zealand or a licensed adviser for that, and to the
institution they apply to for admissions and fees.

Covers: taught vs research master's (Level 9 on the NZQF); what a week
looks like (one NZ credit is designed around ten learning hours, so a
15-credit course expects about 150 hours, most of it independent study);
project-based assessment (a strategic plan, a working database, a simulated
project) and reading the rubric first; the classroom culture shift
(discussion, first names, critical thinking); academic writing and APA 7,
with the common referencing mistakes; academic integrity and generative AI
(follow each course's rules, never submit AI text as your own, declare use,
be able to explain everything); group work in international classes (students
from more than twenty countries across his cohorts); eight habits of students
who do well; questions to ask when choosing a programme; and free lessons to
try before applying. Ends with a nine-question FAQ and a free 30-minute
educational guidance chat (yasassri.me/app/#/consult?type=education).

## Web Products — https://www.yasassri.me/products.html

Research-grade thinking, shipped as software. Beyond the lab, I design and
build full-stack web products that put data, machine learning and clean UX in
front of real users. Snapshot: 4 products in portfolio, 3 live and publicly
usable, AI + ML (local LLM and predictive models), full-stack Python &
JavaScript.

ICT Campus (https://ictcampus.lk) — an online classroom for Sri Lankan A/L
ICT students (Grades 12 and 13) that I founded and teach on. Built with
Next.js, TypeScript and Firebase: phone-number sign-in, live classes through
Zoom with recordings, real-time class chat, timed mock exams, a browser-based
Code Lab, a Sinhala and English interface, and card, bank-slip and cash
payments in one ledger. Its second programme, Campus Ready
(https://ictcampus.lk/campus-ready), teaches students waiting for university
the computer, data and research skills a degree assumes.

**HouseScout** (Live · Property Intelligence · Python, Local AI). A
property-buying dashboard that helps Christchurch home buyers find affordable
homes that match very specific criteria, and stay on top of the market
without endlessly refreshing listing sites. Built for investment-minded
buyers who want to "live in & rent rooms to pay it off fast." Key features:
listings tracker monitoring user-defined criteria; central dashboard with key
metrics; searchable, filterable listings browser; indicative property
valuations & estimates; market insights & analytics on matches; buying-journey
planner; private local AI chat powered by the Gemma model; personalised
settings & saved preferences. Value: turns a scattered, stressful search into
a focused, data-driven workflow — surfacing sub-$500k homes with the right
features (garage, backyard) so first-home buyers and investors can move fast
and buy with confidence. Estimates are indicative, not registered valuations,
and not financial advice. Live: https://ureshan2011.github.io/HouseScout/

**PathFinder** (Live · Study Planning, New Zealand · Static Web,
Client-side). A planning platform for Sri Lankan students applying to
master's and PhD study in New Zealand. Applying for postgraduate study abroad
means piecing the answer together from a dozen half-reliable sources — agent
blogs, forum threads, PDFs three years out of date. PathFinder puts the whole
route in one place: what you qualify for, what it really costs, the visa, and
the move. Key features: seven-stage tracker from assessment to first week; a
five-minute readiness assessment that generates a personalised
month-by-month timeline; 1,716 current NZQF level 8 and 9 qualifications,
searchable by subject, provider and level; 51 providers across 11 subject
areas; a cost calculator in NZ$ and rupees covering tuition, living costs and
visa funds; visa deadlines and settlement guidance; 281 scholarships and
funding sources; mentors already studying in New Zealand. Value: replaces
guesswork and agent fees with the published record — real entry requirements
from the NZQA register, real fees, real visa thresholds — so a student can
see in five minutes whether the route is open to them, and what the next
month should look like. Free to start, no account needed. An independent tool
built from published sources; not affiliated with NZQA, Immigration New
Zealand or any provider, and not immigration advice.
Live: https://ureshan2011.github.io/Pathfinder/

**Faro** (Travel · Python, Machine Learning). A flight-fare timing
assistant that answers the one question every traveller has: book now, or
wait? Faro tracks prices across airlines and uses a model trained on
route-specific history to give a clear, daily Book/Wait call. Key features:
daily fare monitoring across airlines; clear "Book now" vs "Wait"
recommendation; ML trained on route-specific price history; full flight
details (airline, stops, times); refreshes several times a day; aggregates
fares from Google Flights; live weather & currency context; open, publicly
accessible underlying data. Value: flexible travellers save money by booking
in the optimal window, guided by predictive modelling instead of gut feel.
A personal build; not publicly hosted.

**How these are built.** Full-stack web — end-to-end builds in Python and
TypeScript, from data layer to a clean, responsive interface. AI & machine
learning — predictive models and local LLMs wired into products. Data
pipelines — aggregating and cleaning real-world data (listings, fares,
weather, currency) into something dependable. Product UX — designing focused
interfaces that make a complex decision feel simple and trustworthy.

**FAQ.**
Q: Who built HouseScout, PathFinder and Faro? A: All three products were
designed and built by Dr. Yasas Sri Wickramasinghe, a researcher, university
lecturer and software developer based in Christchurch, New Zealand.
Q: Are HouseScout and PathFinder free to use? A: Yes. HouseScout and
PathFinder are both live and free to use directly in a web browser, with no
account required to start. Faro is a personal build and is not publicly
hosted.
Q: What technologies are these products built with? A: HouseScout and Faro
are built with Python, with Faro also using a machine-learning model for
price prediction. PathFinder is a static browser application with no backend
— the assessment, cost calculator and NZQA programme catalogue all run
client-side.
Q: What does HouseScout do? A: HouseScout is a property-buying dashboard for
Christchurch home buyers. It tracks listings against user-defined criteria,
surfaces indicative valuations and market insights, includes a
buying-journey planner, and offers a private local AI assistant powered by
the Gemma model. Estimates are indicative, not registered valuations, and
not financial advice.
Q: How does Faro decide whether to book a flight or wait? A: Faro uses a
machine-learning model trained on route-specific historical fares to predict
how a price is likely to move, then gives a clear "Book now" or "Wait"
recommendation. It monitors fares across airlines and refreshes several
times a day.
Q: Who is PathFinder for? A: Sri Lankan students planning a master's or PhD
in New Zealand. It covers the whole route in one place — a five-minute
readiness assessment, a searchable catalogue of 1,716 current NZQF level 8
and 9 qualifications from 51 providers, real tuition, living and visa-funds
costs in NZ$ and rupees, 281 scholarships, and mentors already studying in
New Zealand.
Q: Where can prospective MBI students learn more? A: See his guide for
prospective students (yasassri.me/students.html) for MBI programme facts,
his teaching approach, and a free consultation link — his own account as the
lecturer who teaches the programme, not an official college page.

## Work With Me — https://www.yasassri.me/work-with-me.html

Research-grade thinking for teams building immersive and learning experiences.
I'm an augmented reality researcher, a senior lecturer and a software engineer.
Organisations bring me in when they need all three at once: to decide whether
an immersive idea is worth building, to find out whether people actually enjoy
using it, or to build a classroom that students don't skip. Proof points: 128
participants across my three published AR user studies; 150,000+ learners on
the MOOC platform I led at the University of Moratuwa; four years as Technical
Lead and Senior Software Engineer at 99X; Sony Interactive Entertainment and
Niantic as industry partners on my AR research at HIT Lab NZ.

**Offer 01 — XR Opportunity Sprint (2–3 weeks).** For tourism operators,
museums and cultural sites, retailers, training providers and game studios
considering AR or VR. Deliverables: a use-case assessment (where AR/VR beats a
screen, and where it doesn't); an experience concept with an interaction flow
grounded in published design guidelines; a technology recommendation (WebAR or
app, Unity, OpenXR, Niantic Lightship, device reach); a prototype plan and
build estimate; and an evaluation plan so the pilot produces evidence.

**Offer 02 — Immersive UX & Playtest Evaluation (3–6 weeks).** For XR
start-ups, game studios and product teams with a prototype or live AR/VR
experience. Study design (lab study, in-the-wild playtest or comparison of
design variants); established measures of presence, simulator sickness, player
experience, workload and usability; session protocol and recruitment including
physical-movement safety; analysis with prioritised recommendations; and a
findings session with the team. Built on three published studies (128
participants), a 36-participant study on trust in shared AR (ACM SUI 2024), and
a VRST 2026 paper on VR presence and motion sickness.

**Offer 03 — EdTech & Engaged-Classroom Advisory (2 weeks to ongoing).** For
private colleges, training providers, universities and EdTech teams. Course
redesign into interactive browser-based lessons; engagement mechanics that
reward persistence; academic-integrity tooling such as attendance fraud
detection; responsible AI in teaching and assessment; and platform build or
review (React, TypeScript, Next.js, Firebase).

**How an engagement runs.** A free 30-minute discovery call; a written scope
with deliverables, timeline and a fixed fee agreed before work starts; regular
working sessions; and a written handover. Remote worldwide or in person in New
Zealand; NDAs welcome. Consulting, workshops and speaking are his independent
practice, not offered on behalf of the University of Canterbury, HIT Lab NZ or
Yoobee College. Discovery-call form (no sign-in):
https://www.yasassri.me/work-with-me.html#discovery

## Case Studies — https://www.yasassri.me/case-studies.html

**Connecting remote players through multiplayer AR (2022–2025).** With Sony
Interactive Entertainment and Niantic as industry partners, at HIT Lab NZ. Three
studies: Study 1 (30 participants) compared Overlay, Window and Tabletop views
of a remote room — Overlay gave the strongest sense of being there; Study 2 (60
participants) ran a remote multiplayer AR hide-and-seek game — a lightweight
view-frustum cue strengthened social connection without avatars or video, and
players used mid-air and vertical space; Study 3 (38 participants) showed
interactive AR mechanics deepened strategic search and engagement when paired
with clear feedback and calibrated constraints. Published across five
peer-reviewed articles including IEEE VR, OzCHI and Elsevier's Entertainment
Computing.

**A state-of-the-art learning management system: a classroom students don't want to skip.** A learning platform he designed and built for the Master of Business Informatics courses he teaches:
one-tap attendance with three fraud checks (shared-IP clustering, GPS outliers
more than 500 m from campus, check-ins within 30 seconds of opening), a live
SQL/Python playground, SQL Race, quiz badges, daily cross-cohort matches and
lecturer analytics — used by 228 students from 24 countries, with 2,500+
attendance records. Four courses were then rebuilt as 39 interactive lessons,
labs and study packs.

**ICT Campus: building a bilingual online school.** Founder, lead teacher and
developer of ictcampus.lk — live Zoom classes with recordings, real-time chat,
timed mock exams and a browser Code Lab covering the full NIE A/L ICT syllabus
in Sinhala and English; free public study pages; and Campus Ready, a 12-week
programme for students waiting to start university.

## The Location-Based AR Design Playbook — https://www.yasassri.me/playbook.html

A free playbook of four evidence-based principles for location-based AR that
connects people across distance, from three user studies with 128 participants
at HIT Lab NZ with Sony Interactive Entertainment as industry partner.
(1) Make the place feel present — use a real-world-scale Overlay for presence
and self-location, Window portals for passing resources between locations, and
high-fidelity 3D scans of the remote space (Study 1, Entertainment Computing
2025). (2) Lightweight presence beats fidelity — show the remote player's
viewpoint in real time, pair it with voice, test minimal cues like a view
frustum before investing in avatars, and design for vertical and mid-air space
(Study 2, IEEE VR 2025 and MDPI MTI 2025). (3) Make AR a core mechanic — embed
AR in the gameplay loop with remotely anchored objects, real-time manipulation
and time pressure calibrated in playtests (Study 3, OzCHI 2025). (4) Guide
without removing the challenge — subtle feedback such as particle trails,
onboarding for the first minutes, and design for safe physical movement. Includes
a 12-question pre-build checklist and a printable PDF:
https://www.yasassri.me/assets/files/ar-design-playbook.pdf — Cite as:
Wickramasinghe, Y. S. (2026). The location-based AR design playbook: Four
evidence-based principles for AR that connects people across distance.

## About — https://www.yasassri.me/about.html

From Colombo lecture halls to Christchurch labs. He studied IT at the
University of Moratuwa (2013–2017), was a Microsoft Imagine Cup runner-up
(2015) and co-founded the AR/VR start-up NavitaZ VR Labs under the MIT Global
Startup Labs programme (2015–2019). He spent four years as a technical lead and
senior software engineer at 99X, lectured at the University of Moratuwa
(2018–2022) and led the Software Engineering strand of its open learning
platform (150,000+ registered learners), then completed a specialisation in
virtual reality at Goldsmiths, University of London. In 2022 he moved to New
Zealand for a fully funded PhD at HIT Lab NZ, University of Canterbury
(2022–2025), researching multiplayer AR with Sony Interactive Entertainment and
Niantic. Today he is a Postdoctoral Researcher at HIT Lab NZ, a Senior Lecturer
at Yoobee College of Creative Innovation, the founder of ICT Campus and the
author of The Collaboration Reflex. What he believes: measure before you argue;
build, test, repeat; and good teaching shouldn't depend on where you live.

## NZGDC 2026 talk — https://www.yasassri.me/nzgdc/

Designing Shared Worlds Across Distance: Lessons from Multiplayer AR Game
Research. NZGDC 2026, Thursday 1 October 2026, 3:00–3:30 PM NZDT, NZ
International Convention Centre, Auckland. What three multiplayer AR games and
128 players taught him about playing together from apart.

**The problem.** Pokémon GO has grossed around US$9 billion in ten years, yet
only about 7% of players say they regularly use the AR camera (Laato et al.,
2021) — the top reason being "it slows me down". Remote play (Remote Raids)
arrived in 2020, Pokémon GO's best year (~US$1.4B), but let players act on a
place without being there. The research question: how can AR make meaningful
use of the real world for synchronous remote multiplayer play? Built in Unity
with Niantic Lightship ARDK on LiDAR iPads, rooms scanned with Scaniverse,
co-designed with Niantic Aotearoa (Wellington), measured with questionnaires,
Tobii eye-tracking glasses, ceiling cameras and interviews.

**Game 1 (30 players): Tabletop, Window or Overlay?** Overlay (the remote room
at 1:1 around you) was preferred by 67% and was the only mode with a
significant lift in feeling present; Window was the most usable, players
called it "the portal", and 8 of 30 tried to walk through it; Tabletop had one
fan. Rule: scale is presence.

**Game 2 (60 players): remote AR hide-and-seek vs real hide-and-seek.** AR
hiders used ceilings and mid-air; hiding took ~40% longer (69s vs 49s), the
"fun" score rose (2.0 vs 0.6 on −3…+3), finding time stayed the same, and 32 of
60 lost track of time. The bright yellow Minion was chosen 15× in AR versus
once in real life (bold objects 1.6× more often) because fiddly thumbstick
placement made players optimise for the controls. A moving view-cone plus
voice created togetherness: 16 players said the cone was enough, 10 wanted an
avatar; strangers cut verbal hints by a third in AR, friends did not.

**Game 3 (38 players): AR-only mechanics.** Resize and camouflage,
multi-object clones, active swapping (with a particle trail for fairness) and
time pressure. One object with no timer gave the highest reward and ease of
use; three objects with no timer the highest engagement; timer plus swapping
the most fun and deepest immersion but the hardest to learn. Players split
roughly 50/50 on wanting a timer.

**Six rules.** (1) If players can switch the AR off, it isn't a mechanic yet.
(2) Scale is presence. (3) Break physics on purpose. (4) A view-cone and a
voice channel buy most of "together". (5) Players optimise for your controls
before your game. (6) Don't choose the pacing — expose the dial. Limitations:
thumbstick placement, Overlay needs an empty room (3 disoriented), arm fatigue
(4), a learning curve for swapping, lag and drift, and first-session data only.
